cls: Antibacterial combinations (dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor with a synergistic partner)
pharm: Group of fixed-dose antibacterials pairing trimethoprim (a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor) with a synergistic agent - most importantly sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) and historically sulfadiazine or sulfametrole - to achieve sequential blockade of bacterial folate synthesis.
quick: Depends on the specific combination; co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) usual adult dose is 160/800 mg every 12 hours
Take with food and plenty of fluids to reduce GI upset and crystalluria
Generally avoided, especially first trimester and near term (folate antagonism, kernicterus risk)
Avoid in jaundiced, ill, premature, or G6PD-deficient infants
Dose-reduce in renal impairment; avoid if severe (CrCl <15-30 depending on agent)
CBC, renal function, electrolytes (potassium), and folate-related effects
summary: Trimethoprim combinations are fixed-dose antibacterials that join trimethoprim with a synergistic partner to block two sequential steps of bacterial folate (and hence DNA) synthesis. The dominant member is co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole), used for urinary tract infections, respiratory infections, and prophylaxis and treatment of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; other historical pairings include trimethoprim-sulfadiazine and trimethoprim-sulfametrole. The combination achieves bactericidal synergy that neither component reliably provides alone. Class hazards reflect the sulfonamide partner (rash, including severe cutaneous reactions, blood dyscrasias, hyperkalemia, and crystalluria) plus trimethoprim's folate and potassium effects. This is a group entry; dose and use depend on the specific product.
indications: Treatment of susceptible urinary tract infections (co-trimoxazole)
Treatment and prophylaxis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (co-trimoxazole)
Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis and other respiratory tract infections caused by susceptible organisms
Other indications specific to the individual combination product (e.g., shigellosis, traveler's diarrhea, toxoplasmosis prophylaxis)

dosage.d: 160 mg TMP / 800 mg SMX every 12 hours
15-20 mg/kg/day of the trimethoprim component in 3-4 divided doses
One double-strength tablet (160/800 mg) once daily or three times weekly
Dose as specified by the individual fixed-dose product (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfadiazine)
dosage.n: Group entry - follow the specific label

admin: Take with food and a full glass of water; maintain good hydration to reduce crystalluria
Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms improve
Adjust the dose in renal impairment and avoid in severe renal failure
Monitor potassium, especially with high doses or in renal impairment, the elderly, or with ACE inhibitors/ARBs
Follow the dosing of the specific combination product, as components and ratios differ
moa: Trimethoprim combinations exploit sequential blockade of the bacterial folate synthesis pathway. The sulfonamide partner (e.g., sulfamethoxazole) is a structural analogue of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) and competitively inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, blocking incorporation of PABA into dihydrofolic acid. Trimethoprim then inhibits the next enzyme, dihydrofolate reductase, preventing conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. Because two consecutive steps are blocked, the combination produces synergistic, often bactericidal, inhibition of bacterial folate-dependent synthesis of nucleic acids and proteins, with selectivity for the bacterial enzymes over the human counterparts.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to trimethoprim or to sulfonamides (for sulfonamide-containing combinations)
Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency
Pregnancy near term and neonates / infants under ~2 months (kernicterus risk with sulfonamide)
relative: Folate deficiency or risk of it
Hyperkalemia or use with other potassium-raising drugs

preg: Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist and sulfonamides displace bilirubin; these combinations are generally avoided in pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester (neural tube and other defect concern) and near term (risk of neonatal kernicterus). Use only if there is no suitable alternative and the benefit outweighs the risk, with folate supplementation considered.
lact: Trimethoprim and sulfonamides pass into breast milk. Avoid in mothers nursing infants who are premature, jaundiced, ill, or G6PD-deficient because of the risk of kernicterus and hemolysis; otherwise use with caution.
renal: Dosage must be reduced according to renal function, and these combinations should generally be avoided in severe renal impairment because of accumulation, hyperkalemia, and the risk of crystalluria. Maintain adequate hydration.
hepatic: Avoid in marked hepatic impairment; sulfonamides can cause hepatotoxicity and hepatocellular necrosis. Monitor liver function in prolonged therapy.

major: Warfarin - potentiation of anticoagulant effect with increased bleeding risk
Methotrexate - additive antifolate effect, increased toxicity (myelosuppression)
ACE inhibitors / ARBs / potassium-sparing diuretics - severe hyperkalemia
moderate: Diuretics (thiazides) - increased risk of thrombocytopenia in the elderly
interactions.food: Take with food and fluids; maintain hydration to reduce crystalluria.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol; a disulfiram-like reaction is uncommon but possible with sulfonamides.
interactions.diagnostics: May falsely elevate serum creatinine (trimethoprim blocks tubular secretion) and interfere with serum methotrexate and some folate assays.

serious: Severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)
rare: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

monitoring: Complete blood count, especially in prolonged or high-dose therapy
Signs of skin reaction (stop at first rash)
counsel: Drink plenty of fluids and take the medicine with food
Stop the medicine and seek care immediately if you develop a rash, blisters, mouth sores, or peeling skin
Finish the full course even if you feel better
Tell your doctor about all other medicines - this combination interacts with blood thinners, diabetes drugs, and several others
Report unusual bruising, bleeding, sore throat, fever, or yellowing of the skin/eyes
pk: Antibacterial activity within hours; clinical improvement over days
Trimethoprim peaks ~1-4 hours after an oral dose; sulfamethoxazole similar
Trimethoprim ~8-10 hours; sulfamethoxazole ~10 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Group/class entry: the clinically dominant member is co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole); follow the specific product label for exact dosing
Synergy comes from sequential blockade of folate synthesis - sulfonamide inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
First-line for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis
Watch for severe skin reactions (SJS/TEN), hyperkalemia (worse with ACE inhibitors/ARBs), and a benign rise in serum creatinine (trimethoprim blocks tubular secretion)
Avoid near term, in neonates, and in folate deficiency or G6PD deficiency
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue your regular schedule - do not double the dose. Keep the doses evenly spaced and complete the full course.
overdose: Overdose can cause nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, confusion, and bone marrow depression (the latter from the antifolate effect of trimethoprim). Management includes gastric decontamination if recent, forcing fluids and urine alkalinization to aid sulfonamide excretion, monitoring of blood counts and electrolytes, and folinic acid (leucovorin) to counteract marrow suppression; hemodialysis is only moderately effective.
